title: Multimodal and longitudinal health data: from models to decisions
html:
Part II · Advanced track · Session 10 of 10

Multimodal and longitudinal health data: from models to decisions

Irregular time, several modalities, mechanistic knowledge, and the step from a prediction to a decision about a dose.

Slides for this session

Starting point

One patient, three years

A kidney-transplant recipient, followed for three years. Tacrolimus trough levels at irregular visits. Creatinine. Doses changed in response to the levels. A CYP3A5 genotype. Biopsy reports. Long gaps without any measurement.

How do we model such a trajectory, and when may a prediction support a decision about the dose?

One patient. A kidney-transplant recipient followed for three years. Tacrolimus trough levels, measured at irregular visits. Creatinine. Doses that were changed in response to those levels. A genotype. Biopsy reports in free text. And long periods with no measurement at all. Two questions. How do we build a model of such a trajectory? And the harder one: suppose the model predicts well. When may that prediction support a decision about the dose? The second question is not a machine-learning question only; it is a causal one.

Learning objectives

By the end of this session you will be able to:

  • Represent irregular, multimodal clinical sequences for a transformer.
  • Combine mechanistic pharmacokinetic models with learned components.
  • Distinguish a prediction from the effect of an intervention.
  • Evaluate a model for clinical usefulness, not only for accuracy.

Four objectives. Represent irregular, multimodal clinical sequences in a form a transformer can read. Combine mechanistic pharmacokinetic models with learned components, in three different ways. Distinguish a prediction from the effect of an intervention, and say what each requires. And evaluate a model for clinical usefulness, not only for accuracy.

Outline

  1. Why clinical trajectories are hardIrregular sampling, informative missingness, feedback
  2. Time in the modelTime-aware embeddings; continuous-time dynamics
  3. Mechanism and learningPharmacokinetic models as priors, simulators and layers
  4. Several modalities, and time to eventFusion strategies; survival objectives
  5. From prediction to decisionCausal questions, usefulness, the human in the loop

Five parts. Why clinical trajectories are hard. How to put time into the model. How to combine mechanism and learning. Several modalities, and time-to-event outcomes. And from prediction to decision: causal questions, usefulness, and the human in the loop.

What makes clinical trajectories hard

Five properties that image and text benchmarks do not have.

PropertyWhat it meansConsequence for modelling
Irregular samplingVisits are not equally spacedEncode real time, not rank
Informative missingnessA test is ordered because someone is worriedThe pattern of measurement is itself a signal, and a source of bias
Several modalitiesNumbers, codes, text, images, at different ratesFusion; robustness to a missing modality
Treatment feedbackDoses are chosen in response to earlier levelsAssociations between dose and outcome are confounded
Censoring and shiftFollow-up ends; centres and assays differSurvival objectives; external validation

Five properties. Irregular sampling: visits are not equally spaced. Informative missingness: a test is ordered because a clinician is worried, so the mere fact that creatinine was measured three times in a week carries information, and it also biases any naive analysis. Several modalities at different rates. Treatment feedback: the dose at one visit was chosen in response to the level at the previous one, so dose and outcome are entangled. And censoring and shift: follow-up ends, patients move, assays change. Each property has a modelling consequence, in the right column. The rest of the session takes them in turn.

What the data look like

When something was measured is information. Resampling to a regular grid throws it away.

This is a schematic of one year for one patient. Three rows: tacrolimus levels, creatinine, dose changes. In the first weeks after transplantation, measurements are dense. Then they thin out. In pink, eleven weeks with no visit at all. In light blue, three creatinine tests within one week, and two dose changes: something happened. If you resample this onto a regular monthly grid and fill the gaps with the last value, you destroy both signals: the gap and the burst. A model for these data must take the timestamps as they are.

A token for a clinical event

What was recorded, its value, and when.

Reading the equation

The code of event i: which drug, which laboratory test, which diagnosis.

Its value, with its unit: a concentration, a dose. φ is a small network or a binning.

Its time: days since transplant, or age. ψ is a continuous encoding, for example sinusoidal.

The token vector that enters the transformer.

Code, value and real time: three embeddings, summed.

The first design decision is the token. An event has three parts. A code: which test, which drug. A value, with a unit. And a time. The token vector is the sum of three embeddings. The code goes through an ordinary embedding table. The value goes through a function phi: a small network, or a discretization into bins followed by an embedding. The time goes through a continuous encoding psi, for instance the sinusoids of session six evaluated at the real time. Delphi-2M does this with age. This design is not settled: how to embed a numeric value so that the model respects its order and its unit is an active research question.

Continuous-time hidden states

Let the state evolve between observations.

Reading the equation

A hidden state defined at every instant, not only at visits.

A neural network that gives the rate of change of the state.

A numerical solver carries the state from one observation time to the next, whatever the gap.

Neural ODEs (Chen et al., 2018); latent ODEs for irregular series (Rubanova et al., 2019).

A compartmental model is a differential equation with a hand-written right-hand side.

A second way to handle irregular time: make the model continuous. Instead of a hidden state updated at each observation, define a state h of t that exists at every instant, and let a neural network give its derivative. To go from one observation to the next, integrate the differential equation with a numerical solver, over whatever gap separates them. This is a neural ordinary differential equation. Gradients flow through the solver. A pharmacologist will recognize the form: a compartmental model is exactly this, with a hand-written right-hand side. That observation leads to the next part.

What pharmacology already knows

A one-compartment model with first-order absorption.

Reading the equation

Amount of drug in the gut; each dose adds to it.

Concentration in blood.

Absorption rate, volume of distribution, clearance: three parameters with a physiological meaning, different in each patient.

Illustrative parameters: 3 mg every 12 h gives a trough near 10 ng/mL and a peak near 19 ng/mL at steady state.

Try it

Here is what pharmacology already knows. A one-compartment model with first-order absorption. Two equations. The amount of drug in the gut decreases at rate k a. The concentration in blood increases with absorption and decreases with elimination, clearance over volume. Three parameters, each with a physiological meaning, each different from patient to patient: that variability is what population pharmacokinetics models. The figure is a simulation with illustrative parameters: three milligrams every twelve hours, a trough near 10 and a peak near 19 nanograms per millilitre. In red, the troughs: the only points a clinician usually sees. A network that ignores this structure must rediscover it from sparse points.

Three ways to combine mechanism and learning

From the most to the least constrained.

1. Learn the parameters

A network maps a patient's covariates to individual CL, V and k_a; the differential equation does the rest. Predictions obey mass balance and extrapolate to new doses.

Deep compartment models (Janssen et al., 2022).

2. Learn a correction

Keep the mechanistic equation and add a neural term for what it misses. The network explains only the residual.

Universal differential equations (Rackauckas et al., 2020).

3. Learn from simulations

Use a published population model to simulate thousands of profiles, and train a flexible model on them; then test on real patients.

Woillard et al., 2021.

The less data you have, the more structure you should impose.

There are three ways to combine the two. One: learn the parameters. A network maps a patient's covariates to individual clearance, volume and absorption rate, and the differential equation produces the concentration curve. The prediction obeys mass balance by construction, and it extrapolates to a dose never seen. Two: learn a correction. Keep the mechanistic equation and add a neural term for what it misses; the network only has to explain the residual. Three: learn from simulations. Take a published population model, simulate thousands of rich profiles, train a flexible model on them, and test on real patients. The choice depends on how much you trust the mechanistic model, and on how much data you have.

Learning from simulations: an example

Tacrolimus exposure estimated by a model trained on simulated profiles (Woillard et al., Pharmacol Res, 2021).

9,000

rich concentration–time profiles simulated from a published population pharmacokinetic model

2 or 3

measured concentrations, plus a few covariates, are enough for the trained model to estimate exposure

4

independent datasets of real transplant patients used for external evaluation

Relative bias under 5 %, relative error under 10 %, comparable to Bayesian estimation, on real patients.

An example of the third route, from the Limoges pharmacology unit. The difficulty with machine learning for exposure estimation is the lack of large databases of full concentration profiles. The authors took a published population pharmacokinetic model of tacrolimus and simulated nine thousand rich profiles. They trained a gradient-boosted model to estimate the area under the curve from two or three concentrations and a few covariates. Then they evaluated it on four independent datasets of real transplant patients with rich sampling. Relative bias was under five percent and relative root-mean-square error under ten percent, comparable to Bayesian estimation. Mechanistic knowledge supplied the training data; real patients supplied the verdict.

Fusing modalities

Where in the model the modalities meet.

StrategyHowStrengthWeakness
Early fusionConcatenate the inputsSimple; captures low-level interactionsNeeds every modality, aligned
Intermediate fusionOne encoder per modality, then cross-attention or a shared transformerFlexible; the current defaultMore parameters; more data
Late fusionOne model per modality; combine the predictionsRobust to a missing modalityMisses interactions
Contrastive alignmentPre-train encoders so that paired modalities matchUses unlabelled pairsAligns only what the modalities share

A patient is described by numbers, codes, text and images. Where should the modalities meet? Early fusion concatenates inputs: simple, but it needs every modality to be present and aligned. Late fusion trains one model per modality and combines predictions: robust when a modality is missing, blind to interactions. Intermediate fusion is the current default: one encoder per modality, then tokens from all modalities enter a shared transformer, or attend to each other through cross-attention. And contrastive alignment, from session seven, pre-trains the encoders on unlabelled pairs. In every case, train with modalities randomly dropped: in the clinic, something is always missing.

Each modality keeps its own encoder; the interaction is learned.

Intermediate fusion as a diagram. On the left, three sources: the sequence of doses, levels and laboratory values; the reports; the biopsy images. Each has its own encoder, often a pre-trained foundation model adapted as in session nine. Their outputs are sequences of tokens. A fusion transformer lets the tokens of all modalities attend to each other. On the right, several heads read the fused representation: the risk of graft loss, the next drug level, a phenotype. Training several heads together is multi-task learning, and it usually helps when labels for each task are scarce.

Time-to-event outcomes

Graft loss is not a yes-or-no label: follow-up may end first.

Reading the equation

The time of the event, in discrete intervals (months, for instance).

The hazard: the probability that the event occurs in interval t, given that it has not occurred before.

1 if the event was observed for patient i; 0 if follow-up ended first (censoring).

Every interval survived contributes to the likelihood, for censored patients too.

Many clinical outcomes are times to an event, and for many patients the event has not happened when follow-up ends: they are censored. Treating them as negatives is wrong. A simple and effective approach uses discrete time. The network outputs a hazard for each interval: the probability that the event occurs in that interval given that it has not occurred before. The likelihood has two parts. For every interval a patient survived, the log of one minus the hazard. And if the event was observed, delta equals one, the log of the hazard at the event time. Censored patients contribute everything we know: that they survived until they left. Evaluate with a concordance index and time-dependent calibration.

A prediction is not the effect of an intervention

The quantity a dosing decision needs.

Reading the equation

Potential outcomes: what would happen to the same patient with the dose changed, and without. Only one is ever observed.

The effect of the intervention for patients with characteristics x.

A predictive model estimates E[Y | X, A] under the prescribing habits that produced the data. It answers “what will happen”, not “what if I change the dose”.

Y · outcome

the effect we want

L opens a second path from A to Y: confounding by indication.

Sicker patients were given different doses: that is confounding by indication.

Now the delicate step. A dosing decision needs to know what would happen if the dose were changed, compared with not changing it. Formally: the difference between two potential outcomes for the same patient, Y of one and Y of zero. Only one of them is ever observed. A predictive model estimates something else: the expected outcome given the characteristics and the dose that was actually chosen, under the prescribing habits that generated the data. The diagram shows the problem. The last level and renal function influence the dose the clinician chose, and they also influence the outcome. A model will find that high doses go with poor outcomes, simply because sicker patients received higher doses.

When may a prediction support a decision?

Three routes from observational data to an interventional claim.

  • State the assumptions. No unmeasured confounding; every patient could have received either option; well-defined interventions.
  • Emulate a target trial. Write the protocol of the trial you would have run, then analyse the observational data accordingly (Hernán and Robins, 2016).
  • Use the mechanism. A pharmacokinetic model does answer “what if the dose were 4 mg”, for exposure. Linking exposure to clinical outcome remains the open part.
  • Then test prospectively.

So when may a prediction support a decision? Three routes. First, state the assumptions under which an effect can be estimated from observational data: no unmeasured confounding, positivity, meaning every kind of patient could have received either option, and well-defined interventions. Second, emulate a target trial: write the protocol of the randomized trial you would like to run, eligibility, treatment strategies, time zero, outcome, and analyse the observational data to mimic it. Third, use the mechanism. A pharmacokinetic model genuinely answers a what-if question about exposure, because it encodes how dose produces concentration. The link from exposure to clinical outcome is the open part. And in every case: prospective evaluation.

Evaluation that matters

From statistical performance to clinical usefulness.

LevelQuestionTools
DiscriminationDoes it rank patients correctly?AUC, concordance index
CalibrationDo predicted risks match observed frequencies?Calibration curve, by subgroup
TransportabilityDoes it work elsewhere, later?External and temporal validation
Clinical usefulnessDoes acting on it do more good than harm?Decision-curve analysis: net benefit
ImpactDo patients do better when clinicians have it?Prospective study; randomized if possible

Report according to TRIPOD+AI (Collins et al., 2024).

Evaluation has levels, and most publications stop at the first. Discrimination: does the model rank patients correctly? Calibration: do predicted risks match observed frequencies, overall and in subgroups? Transportability: does it work in another centre, in a later period? Clinical usefulness: if clinicians act on it at a given risk threshold, does that do more good than harm? And impact: do patients actually do better when clinicians have the tool? That last level needs a prospective study. Reporting should follow the TRIPOD plus AI statement, and the course on responsible AI treats the first three levels in detail.

Net benefit

One number for clinical usefulness at a chosen risk threshold.

Reading the equation

The risk threshold above which one would act: it encodes how many false alarms one accepts per true case.

True and false positives when acting on all patients whose predicted risk exceeds the threshold.

The number of patients.

Compare with two default strategies: act on everyone, act on no one (net benefit 0).

Decision-curve analysis gives one number for usefulness. Choose a risk threshold, p t, above which you would act; say twenty percent. That choice encodes a trade-off: at twenty percent you accept four false alarms for one true case. The net benefit is the proportion of true positives minus the proportion of false positives weighted by that exchange rate. It is expressed in true positives per patient. Then compare with two strategies that need no model: act on everyone, and act on no one, whose net benefit is zero. A model is useful at a threshold only if it beats both. Plot this across thresholds and you have a decision curve.

A model output is an input to a decision, not the decision.

A system that can say “I do not know” is more useful than one that is slightly more accurate.

The last diagram. A model output is an input to a decision. The model produces a prediction with its uncertainty: a calibrated risk, or a conformal interval from session nine. If the uncertainty is too large, or the patient is unlike the training population, the system abstains and says why. Otherwise the suggestion is shown together with its interval, never as a bare number. The clinician decides and may overrule. The decision and the outcome are logged, which feeds both the evaluation and the next version of the model. The design question is not only accuracy. It is whether the clinician can tell when to trust the output, and automation bias is the known risk.

Your turn

Design a study, compute a benefit

  1. You want to predict the next tacrolimus trough level from a patient's record. Specify: the tokens; how you split the data; the baseline you must beat; your primary metric.
  2. Name one causal pitfall if the model is later used to choose the dose.
  3. A rejection-risk model is applied to 1,000 patients, 200 of whom will have the event. At a threshold of 20 %, it flags 350 patients: 150 true positives and 200 false positives. Compute its net benefit.
  4. Compute the net benefit of treating everyone at the same threshold. Is the model useful?

Time: 12 minutes · Material: Paper and a calculator · Deliverable: A five-line study design and two net benefits

Show the solution
  • Tokens: events (code, value, real time), with dose and time since last dose. Split: by patient, and by period or centre for the test set.
  • Baseline: population pharmacokinetic model with Bayesian estimation; also “last value carried forward”. Metric: relative error in ng/mL terms, with calibration of the intervals.
  • Pitfall: doses in the data were chosen from earlier levels. The model learned to predict under that policy, not what a different dose would do.
  • Model: 150/1000 − (200/1000) × (0.2/0.8) = 0.15 − 0.05 = 0.10. Treat all: 0.20 − 0.80 × 0.25 = 0. The model is useful at this threshold.

Net benefit 0.10: equivalent to finding 100 true cases per 1,000 patients with no false alarm.

Solutions. Tokens: events with a code, a value and a real time, and make sure the dose and the time since the last dose are represented. Split by patient, and keep a later period or another centre for the test. The baseline to beat is the population pharmacokinetic model with Bayesian estimation, the current standard; and also the trivial rule, last value carried forward. Metric: relative error, with calibrated intervals. The pitfall: doses in the data were chosen from earlier levels, so the model predicts under that policy. For the numbers: zero point one five minus zero point two times one quarter is zero point one. Treating everyone gives zero point two minus zero point eight times one quarter: zero. The model is useful at that threshold.

Self-check

One correct answer per question.

1. Resampling an irregular record onto a monthly grid mainly loses:

Gaps and bursts of testing are signals.

2. A model trained on observational data finds that higher doses predict worse outcomes. The likely reason is:

Sicker patients were given higher doses.

3. A censored patient contributes to a discrete-time survival loss:

Every survived interval adds a log(1 − hazard) term.

Key takeaways

  1. Encode events as code, value and real time; do not resample away the timestamps.
  2. Use the mechanism: learn parameters, learn a correction, or learn from simulations.
  3. Fuse modalities at an intermediate level, and train with modalities dropped.
  4. A prediction answers “what will happen”; a decision needs “what if”. Say which one you claim.
  5. Evaluate up to usefulness: external validation, calibration, net benefit, and a human who can overrule.

Five takeaways for this session, and in a sense for the course. Encode events as code, value and real time. Use the mechanism: learn its parameters, learn a correction to it, or learn from its simulations. Fuse modalities at an intermediate level, and train with modalities dropped. A prediction answers what will happen; a decision needs what if: say which one you claim. And evaluate up to usefulness, with a human who can overrule.
